concepts.label: The Long History of a Global World
concepts.cardText: The making of the global world has a long history of trade, migration, people in search of work and the movement of capital, not just the last 50 years of globalisation. All through history human societies have become steadily more interlinked. From ancient times travellers, traders, priests and pilgrims travelled vast distances for knowledge, opportunity and spiritual fulfilment, or to escape persecution, carrying goods, money, values, skills, ideas, inventions and even germs and diseases. As early as 3000 BCE an active coastal trade linked the Indus valley civilisations with West Asia, cowries from the Maldives reached China and East Africa, and the long-distance spread of disease-carrying germs may be traced to the seventh century.

concepts.causeChain: People travelled for knowledge, opportunity and escape -> they carried goods, ideas, skills and even diseases -> trade links such as the Indus valley coastal trade and the cowrie trade show global connection existed long before modern globalisation

keyPoints.text: When we talk of ‘globalisation’ we often refer to an economic system that has emerged since the last 50 years or so. But as you will see in this chapter, the making of the global world has a long history – of trade, of migration, of people in search of work, the movement of capital, and much else.

concepts.label: Silk Routes Link the World
concepts.cardText: The silk routes are a good example of vibrant pre-modern trade and cultural links between distant parts of the world. The name points to the importance of west-bound Chinese silk cargoes. Historians have identified several silk routes, over land and by sea, knitting together vast regions of Asia and linking Asia with Europe and northern Africa; they existed since before the Christian Era and thrived almost till the fifteenth century. Chinese pottery, textiles and spices from India and Southeast Asia travelled the same route, and precious metals, gold and silver, flowed from Europe to Asia. Trade and cultural exchange always went hand in hand: early Christian missionaries and later Muslim preachers travelled this route, and Buddhism spread from eastern India along it.

concepts.label: Food Travels: Spaghetti and Potato
concepts.cardText: Food offers many examples of long-distance cultural exchange. Traders and travellers introduced new crops to the lands they travelled, and it is believed that noodles travelled west from China to become spaghetti. Many common foods such as potatoes, soya, groundnuts, maize, tomatoes, chillies and sweet potatoes were not known to our ancestors until about five centuries ago; they were introduced in Europe and Asia only after Christopher Columbus accidentally discovered the Americas, and many came from America's original inhabitants. New crops could make the difference between life and death: Europe's poor ate better and lived longer with the potato, but Ireland's poorest peasants became so dependent on it that when disease destroyed the crop in the mid-1840s, hundreds of thousands died of starvation.

concepts.label: Conquest, Disease and Trade
concepts.cardText: The pre-modern world shrank greatly in the sixteenth century after European sailors found a sea route to Asia and crossed the western ocean to America. The Indian Ocean had long known a bustling trade, with the Indian subcontinent central to the flows; the Europeans helped expand or redirect some towards Europe. America, cut off for millions of years, now transformed trade and lives everywhere, and silver from Peru and Mexico enhanced Europe's wealth and financed its trade with Asia. The Spanish and Portuguese conquest was not just a result of superior firepower: the most powerful weapon was the germs, such as smallpox, that conquerors carried. America's original inhabitants had no immunity because of long isolation, so smallpox killed whole communities, paving the way for conquest. Guns could be turned against invaders, but not diseases to which the conquerors were mostly immune. Meanwhile China restricted overseas contacts, and with the rising importance of the Americas the centre of world trade moved westwards to Europe.

concepts.label: Three Flows of International Economic Exchange
concepts.cardText: The world changed profoundly in the nineteenth century. Economists identify three types of movement or flows within international economic exchanges. The first is the flow of trade, which in the nineteenth century referred largely to trade in goods such as cloth or wheat. The second is the flow of labour, the migration of people in search of employment. The third is the movement of capital for short-term or long-term investments over long distances. All three flows were closely interwoven and affected people's lives more deeply than ever before, though labour migration was often more restricted than goods or capital flows.

concepts.label: A World Economy Takes Shape: The Corn Laws
concepts.cardText: In nineteenth-century Britain, self-sufficiency in food meant lower living standards and social conflict. Population growth and expanding towns raised demand for food grains and pushed up prices; under pressure from landed groups the government restricted corn imports through the Corn Laws. Unhappy with high food prices, industrialists and urban dwellers forced the abolition of the Corn Laws. Food could now be imported more cheaply than it could be produced in Britain, so British agriculture could not compete, vast areas were left uncultivated and thousands were thrown out of work and flocked to cities or migrated overseas. Lower food prices raised consumption and, with faster industrial growth, more food imports; lands were cleared in Eastern Europe, Russia, America and Australia, with railways, harbours, settlements, capital from London and labour. Nearly 50 million people emigrated from Europe to America and Australia, and by 1890 a global agricultural economy had taken shape.

concepts.label: Canal Colonies and Regional Specialisation
concepts.cardText: Some of this dramatic change occurred on a smaller scale in west Punjab, where the British Indian government built a network of irrigation canals to transform semi-desert wastes into fertile agricultural lands that could grow wheat and cotton for export. The Canal Colonies, as the irrigated areas were called, were settled by peasants from other parts of Punjab. A similar story can be told for cotton, whose cultivation expanded worldwide to feed British textile mills, and for rubber. So rapidly did regional specialisation in commodities develop that between 1820 and 1914 world trade is estimated to have multiplied 25 to 40 times, with nearly 60 per cent of it in primary products such as wheat, cotton and coal.

concepts.label: Role of Technology and the Meat Trade
concepts.cardText: Railways, steamships and the telegraph were important inventions without which the transformed nineteenth-century world is unimaginable, but technological advances were often the result of larger social, political and economic factors. Colonisation stimulated new investments and improvements in transport, such as faster railways, lighter wagons and larger ships, which moved food more cheaply and quickly. The meat trade shows this: until the 1870s animals were shipped live from America to Europe, took up ship space and often died or lost weight, so meat was an expensive luxury beyond the European poor. concepts.label: Late Nineteenth-Century Colonialism
concepts.cardText: Trade flourished and markets expanded in the late nineteenth century, but there was a darker side: in many parts of the world, the expansion of trade and a closer relationship with the world economy also meant a loss of freedoms and livelihoods. Late-nineteenth-century European conquests produced painful economic, social and ecological changes through which colonised societies were brought into the world economy. In 1885 the big European powers met in Berlin to complete the carving up of Africa between them, drawing borders almost with a ruler. Britain and France made vast additions to their overseas territories, Belgium and Germany became new colonial powers, and the US became one in the late 1890s by taking over colonies held by Spain. Explorers like Henry Morton Stanley went with arms and local labourers, and geographical exploration was not an innocent search for scientific information but directly linked to imperial projects.

concepts.label: Rinderpest, or the Cattle Plague
concepts.cardText: In Africa in the 1890s a fast-spreading cattle plague, rinderpest, had a terrifying impact on livelihoods and the local economy. Historically Africa had abundant land and a small population, and land and livestock sustained livelihoods so people rarely worked for wages. Europeans, attracted by Africa's land and minerals, wanted to set up plantations and mines but found a shortage of labour willing to work for wages. Employers imposed heavy taxes payable only by wage work, changed inheritance laws so only one family member inherited land and the others were pushed into the labour market, and confined mineworkers in compounds. Rinderpest then arrived in the late 1880s with infected cattle imported from British Asia to feed Italian soldiers invading Eritrea; it spread west like forest fire, reached the Atlantic coast in 1892 and the Cape five years later, killing 90 per cent of the cattle. The loss of cattle destroyed African livelihoods, and planters, mine owners and colonial governments monopolised the scarce cattle to force Africans into the labour market, enabling Europeans to conquer and subdue Africa.

concepts.label: Indentured Labour Migration from India
concepts.cardText: Indentured labour migration illustrates the two-sided nature of the nineteenth-century world: faster growth and great misery, higher incomes for some and poverty for others, technological advances and new forms of coercion. Indentured labourers were bonded labourers under contract to work for an employer for a fixed time to pay off their passage, and Indian indentured labourers were promised return travel after five years on a plantation. Most came from eastern Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, central India and the dry districts of Tamil Nadu, where cottage industries declined, land rents rose and lands were cleared for mines and plantations, so the poor fell into debt and were forced to migrate. They went to the Caribbean islands, Mauritius, Fiji, Ceylon, Malaya and Assam's tea plantations. Agents paid a small commission tempted migrants with false information and sometimes abducted them. Conditions were harsh with few legal rights, so indenture was called a 'new system of slavery'. Workers escaped into the wilds or developed new cultural forms such as Hosay, Rastafarianism and chutney music. Nationalist leaders opposed the system and it was abolished in 1921.

concepts.label: Indian Entrepreneurs Abroad
concepts.cardText: Growing food and other crops for the world market required capital. Large plantations could borrow it from banks and markets, but the humble peasant could not, so Indian bankers stepped in. The Shikaripuri Shroffs and Nattukottai Chettiars were among the groups of bankers and traders who financed export agriculture in Central and Southeast Asia, using their own funds or funds borrowed from European banks. Indian traders and moneylenders also followed European colonisers into Africa, while Hyderabadi Sindhi traders ventured beyond European colonies and from the 1860s established flourishing emporia at busy ports worldwide.

concepts.label: Indian Trade, Colonialism and the Global System
concepts.cardText: Historically, fine Indian cottons were exported to Europe. With industrialisation British cotton manufacture expanded and industrialists pressurised the government to restrict cotton imports; tariffs were imposed on cloth imports into Britain and the inflow of fine Indian cotton declined. British manufacturers also sought overseas markets, so Indian textiles faced stiff competition in international markets: the share of cotton textiles in India's exports fell from some 30 per cent around 1800 to 15 per cent by 1815 and below 3 per cent by the 1870s, while exports of raw materials like raw cotton (5 per cent to 35 per cent between 1812 and 1871) and indigo rose, and opium shipments to China became for a while India's largest export. British manufactures flooded the Indian market, and since British exports to India were worth much more than imports from India, Britain had a trade surplus with India, which it used to settle its deficits with other countries in a multilateral settlement system and to pay home charges.

concepts.label: Wartime Transformations
concepts.cardText: The First World War (1914-18) was mainly fought in Europe but its impact was felt around the world, plunging the first half of the twentieth century into a crisis that took over three decades to overcome. It was fought between the Allies (Britain, France and Russia, later joined by the US) and the Central Powers (Germany, Austria-Hungary and Ottoman Turkey). It was the first modern industrial war, using machine guns, tanks, aircraft and chemical weapons on a massive scale, with 9 million dead and 20 million injured, mostly men of working age. These deaths and injuries reduced the able-bodied workforce in Europe, and household incomes declined after the war. Industries were restructured to produce war-related goods, and women stepped into jobs that earlier only men did. The war snapped economic links between powers; Britain borrowed heavily from US banks and the public, and the US was transformed from an international debtor to an international creditor.

concepts.label: Post-war Recovery
concepts.cardText: Post-war economic recovery proved difficult. Britain, the world's leading pre-war economy, faced a prolonged crisis: while it was preoccupied with war, industries had developed in India and Japan, and afterwards it found it difficult to recapture its dominance in the Indian market or to compete with Japan. It was also burdened with huge external debts after borrowing from the US. When the war boom ended, production contracted and unemployment increased, and with reduced war expenditure there were huge job losses; in 1921 one in every five British workers was out of work. Agricultural economies were also in crisis: when eastern Europe's wheat supply was disrupted in the war, production expanded in Canada, America and Australia, but when eastern Europe revived it created a glut, grain prices fell, rural incomes declined and farmers fell deeper into debt.

concepts.label: Rise of Mass Production and Consumption
concepts.cardText: In the US, recovery was quicker, and mass production became a characteristic feature of industrial production in the 1920s. The car manufacturer Henry Ford adapted the assembly line of a Chicago slaughterhouse to his car plant in Detroit. The assembly line forced workers to repeat a single task mechanically at a pace dictated by the conveyor belt, increasing output per worker; Ford's cars came off the line at three-minute intervals, and the T-Model was the first mass-produced car. Workers quit in large numbers, so Ford doubled the daily wage to $5 in January 1914 and banned trade unions, recovering the high wage by speeding up the line. Mass production lowered costs and prices, and higher wages let more workers buy durable consumer goods such as cars, refrigerators and washing machines, often on hire purchase. Car production rose from 2 million in 1919 to more than 5 million in 1929. A housing and consumer boom created a cycle of higher employment, incomes, consumption and investment, and in 1923 the US became the largest overseas lender.

concepts.label: The Great Depression
concepts.cardText: The Great Depression began around 1929 and lasted till the mid-1930s, bringing catastrophic declines in production, employment, incomes and trade; agricultural regions were the worst affected because the fall in agricultural prices was greater and more prolonged than in industrial prices. It was caused by several factors. First, agricultural overproduction remained a problem and worsened with falling prices: farmers expanded production to maintain income, worsening the glut and pushing prices down further, so farm produce rotted for lack of buyers. Second, in the mid-1920s many countries financed investments through US loans, but US lenders panicked at the first sign of trouble; overseas loans of over $1 billion in early 1928 fell to a quarter a year later, causing an acute crisis in countries that depended on them. The withdrawal of US loans led to bank failures and the collapse of the British pound sterling in Europe and intensified the slump in agricultural prices in Latin America, and the US doubling its import duties dealt a severe blow to world trade. In the US itself farms could not sell harvests, households were ruined and the banking system collapsed: by 1933 over 4,000 banks had closed and about 110,000 companies had collapsed between 1929 and 1932.

concepts.label: India and the Great Depression
concepts.cardText: The impact of the depression on India shows how integrated the global economy had become: tremors of a crisis in one part of the world were quickly relayed to others. Colonial India had become an exporter of agricultural goods and importer of manufactures, so the depression immediately affected trade: India's exports and imports nearly halved between 1928 and 1934, and wheat prices fell by 50 per cent. Peasants and farmers suffered more than urban dwellers because the colonial government refused to reduce revenue demands even though agricultural prices fell sharply; those producing for the world market were worst hit. Bengal's jute growers saw the price of raw jute crash more than 60 per cent as gunny exports collapsed, and fell deeper into debt. Across India peasants' indebtedness increased; they used up savings, mortgaged land and sold jewellery, and India became an exporter of precious metals, notably gold, which helped speed up Britain's recovery but did little for the Indian peasant. Rural India was seething with unrest when Gandhi launched the civil disobedience movement in 1931. The depression proved less grim for urban India, as people with fixed incomes found everything cost less and industrial investment grew with tariff protection.

concepts.label: The Second World War and Post-War Reconstruction
concepts.cardText: The Second World War broke out a mere two decades after the First, between the Axis powers (mainly Nazi Germany, Japan and Italy) and the Allies (Britain, France, the Soviet Union and the US), and was waged for six years on many fronts. At least 60 million people, about 3 per cent of the world's 1939 population, were killed directly or indirectly. Unlike earlier wars, most deaths took place outside the battlefields, and many more civilians than soldiers died. Vast parts of Europe and Asia were devastated and reconstruction promised to be long and difficult. Two influences shaped post-war reconstruction: the US's emergence as the dominant economic, political and military power in the Western world, and the dominance of the Soviet Union, which had made huge sacrifices to defeat Nazi Germany and transformed itself from a backward agricultural country into a world power while the capitalist world was trapped in the Great Depression.

concepts.label: Post-war Settlement and the Bretton Woods Institutions
concepts.cardText: Economists and politicians drew two key lessons from inter-war experience. First, an industrial society based on mass production cannot be sustained without mass consumption, which needs high and stable incomes and therefore steady, full employment; since markets alone cannot guarantee full employment, governments must intervene to minimise fluctuations of price, output and employment. Second, the goal of full employment could only be achieved if governments had power to control flows of goods, capital and labour. The main aim of the post-war system was to preserve economic stability and full employment in the industrial world. Its framework was agreed at the United Nations Monetary and Financial Conference at Bretton Woods, New Hampshire, in July 1944, which established the International Monetary Fund (IMF) to deal with external surpluses and deficits and the World Bank to finance post-war reconstruction. These Bretton Woods institutions began operating in 1947, are controlled by the Western industrial powers, and the US has an effective veto. The Bretton Woods system was based on fixed exchange rates, with currencies pegged to the dollar and the dollar anchored to gold at $35 per ounce.

concepts.cardText: The Bretton Woods system inaugurated an era of unprecedented growth of trade and incomes for the Western industrial nations and Japan. These decades also saw the worldwide spread of technology and enterprise: developing countries in a hurry to catch up invested vast amounts of capital and imported industrial plant and equipment with modern technology.

concepts.label: Decolonisation, Independence and the G-77
concepts.cardText: When the Second World War ended, large parts of the world were still under European colonial rule. Over the next two decades most colonies in Asia and Africa emerged as free, independent nations, but they were overburdened by poverty and lack of resources, and handicapped by long colonial rule. The IMF and World Bank were designed to meet the financial needs of industrial countries and were not equipped to cope with poverty in the former colonies, though from the late 1950s they began to shift attention to developing countries. Ironically, the newly independent countries came under the guidance of international agencies dominated by former colonial powers, which still controlled vital resources, and large corporations often secured rights to exploit natural resources very cheaply. Most developing countries did not benefit from the fast growth of the 1950s and 1960s, so they organised themselves as the Group of 77 (G-77) to demand a new international economic order (NIEO): real control over their natural resources, more development assistance, fairer prices for raw materials and better access for their manufactures in developed countries' markets.

concepts.label: End of Bretton Woods and the Beginning of Globalisation
concepts.cardText: From the 1960s the rising costs of its overseas involvements weakened the US's finances and competitive strength. The dollar no longer commanded confidence as the world's principal currency and could not maintain its value in relation to gold, which led to the collapse of fixed exchange rates and the introduction of floating exchange rates. From the mid-1970s developing countries were forced to borrow from Western commercial banks and private lenders instead of international institutions, leading to periodic debt crises, lower incomes and increased poverty, especially in Africa and Latin America. Unemployment began rising in the industrial world from the mid-1970s, and from the late 1970s multinational corporations (MNCs) began shifting production to low-wage Asian countries. Large companies operating in several countries, MNCs had spread in the 1950s and 1960s partly because high import tariffs forced them to produce locally. New economic policies in China and the collapse of the Soviet Union brought many countries back into the world economy, and low wages made China an attractive destination for MNCs competing for world markets. The relocation of industry stimulated world trade and capital flows and transformed the world's economic geography as India, China and Brazil underwent rapid change.
